analysis.one_liner: Requires new cars to have systems that detect children or pets left in the back seat.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021, despite 56 bipartisan cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Department of Transportation to write a rule requiring every new passenger vehicle weighing 10,000 pounds or less to carry a system that detects a child or pet in the back seat after the engine is shut off, and then sounds an alarm inside and outside the car. States would have had to spend part of their federal highway safety money on public education about the dangers of leaving people in parked cars, and the Transportation Department would have had to commission an independent study on retrofitting older vehicles. The bill was introduced in June 2019 and referred to two House committees, but neither committee ever acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children, pet owners, and caregivers. On average 38 children a year die of heatstroke after being left in or gaining access to a vehicle, and at least 52 died in 2018; the bill's findings state that technology to detect a child in the rear seat already exists.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with young children and pet owners

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Transportation Department to issue a rule, within two years, mandating that all new vehicles of 10,000 pounds or less have a system that detects an occupant in a rear seat after the engine is turned off and issues an audible, visual, and haptic (vibration) warning [S2][S3].
Directs states to use a portion of federal highway safety funding to educate the public on the risks of leaving an occupant in a vehicle [S3].
Requires an independent study of retrofitting existing vehicles with occupant-detection technology, with recommendations to help consumers choose products [S2][S3].
The bill's findings cite an average of 38 child heatstroke deaths per year, at least 889 deaths from 1990 to 2018, and note the detection technology already exists [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Buyers of new vehicles, through modest price increases to cover the required detection and alert hardware, and automakers, who bear the compliance and engineering costs of the mandate.

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies only to new vehicles; the roughly 280 million vehicles already on the road would not be covered, which is why the bill orders a study on retrofitting older cars rather than requiring it [S2][S3].

A blanket mandate raises the price of every new car, including for buyers without young children or pets, and detection systems can in practice produce false alarms that train drivers to ignore them — a cost an honest supporter of the bill would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and large for the families affected: dozens of child deaths a year, against a per-vehicle hardware cost spread across all new-car purchases. The main design weakness is that it does nothing for the existing vehicle fleet until a study is completed, and no retrofit requirement follows from that study.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2019 and referred to two House committees and their subcommittees, but neither committee ever brought it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 28, 2019, with Rep. Tim Ryan as sponsor and Reps. Schakowsky and King of New York as original cosponsors [S1][S3].

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, and within days to the Consumer Protection and Commerce and Highways and Transit subcommittees [S5].
It gathered 56 cosponsors, 54 Democrats and 2 Republicans, but no committee reported it out and it never received a House floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers are better off because the bill died; they avoided a federal mandate to install rear-seat occupant-detection systems in every new vehicle. Families who lose children to vehicle heatstroke gain nothing from the outcome.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan but skewed Democratic: 54 of 231 House Democrats and 2 of 197 House Republicans signed on, and no vote was ever held.

industries.note: The bill would have mandated occupant-detection and alert systems in all new vehicles of 10,000 pounds or less, imposing engineering and hardware compliance costs that automakers would pass to buyers. Its failure left them free of the requirement. With the bill dead, the industry's interest in avoiding the mandate ran against a safety measure aimed at preventing dozens of child deaths a year.

industries.industry: Aftermaker occupant-detection and retrofit technology makers
industries.note: The bill orders an independent study of retrofitting existing vehicles and consumer guidance on choosing those products, which could have grown the aftermarket market. The study also required performance recommendations to ensure the products work in real-world conditions.
